{{short description|Lens with a thickness that is negligible}}
[[Image:Lens1.svg|thumb|A lens may be considered a thin lens if its thickness is much less than the radii of curvature of its surfaces ({{math|{{mvar|d}} ≪ {{pipe}}{{mvar|R}}<sub>1</sub>{{pipe}}}} and {{math|{{mvar|d}} ≪ {{pipe}}{{mvar|R}}<sub>2</sub>{{pipe}}}}).|300px]]

In [[optics]], a '''thin lens''' is a [[lens (optics)|lens]] with a thickness (distance along the [[optical axis]] between the two surfaces of the lens) that is negligible compared to the [[radius of curvature (optics)|radii of curvature]] of the lens surfaces. Lenses whose thickness is not negligible are sometimes called ''thick lenses''.

The '''thin lens approximation''' ignores optical effects due to the thickness of lenses and simplifies [[Ray tracing (physics)|ray tracing]] calculations. It is often combined with the [[paraxial approximation]] in techniques such as [[ray transfer matrix analysis]].

==Focal length==
The focal length, ''f'', of a lens in air is given by the [[lensmaker's equation]]:
:<math>\frac{1}{f} = (n-1) \left[ \frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{(n-1)d}{n R_1 R_2} \right],</math>
where ''n'' is the [[index of refraction]] of the lens material, ''R''<sub>1</sub> and ''R''<sub>2</sub> are the [[Radius of curvature (optics)|radii of curvature]] of the two surfaces, and ''d'' is the thickness of the lens. Here ''R''<sub>1</sub> is taken to be positive if the first surface is convex, and negative if the surface is concave. The signs are reversed for the back surface of the lens: ''R''<sub>2</sub> is positive if the surface is concave, and negative if it is convex. This is an arbitrary [[sign convention]]; some authors choose different signs for the radii, which changes the equation for the focal length.

For a thin lens, ''d'' is much smaller than one of the radii of curvature (either ''R''<sub>1</sub> or ''R''<sub>2</sub>). In these conditions, the last term of the Lensmaker's equation becomes negligible, and the focal length of a thin lens in air can be approximated by<ref>
{{cite book
 |last=Hecht |first=Eugene
 |year=1987
 |title=Optics
 |at=§ 5.2.3 |edition=2nd
 |publisher=[[Addison Wesley]]
 |isbn=0-201-11609-X
}}</ref><ref name=pt/>
:<math>\frac{1}{f} \approx \left(n-1\right)\left[ \frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2} \right].</math>
<!--
  CAUTION TO EDITORS: This equation depends on an arbitrary sign convention
  (explained on the page). If the signs don't match your textbook, your book
  is probably using a different sign convention.
-->

=== Derivation using Snell's law ===
[[File:Half lens.svg|thumb|Refraction of a thin planoconvex lens]]
Consider a thin lens with a first surface of radius <math display="inline">R</math> and a flat rear surface, made of material with index of refraction <math display="inline">n</math>.

Applying [[Snell's law]], light entering the first surface is refracted according to <math>\sin i = n \sin r_1</math>, where <math>i</math> is the angle of incidence on the interface and <math>r_1</math> is the angle of refraction. 

For the second surface, <math>n \sin r_2 = \sin e </math>, where <math>r_2</math> is the angle of incidence and <math>e</math> is the angle of refraction.

For small angles, <math display=inline>\sin x \approx x</math>. The geometry of the problem then gives:

<math display=block>\begin{align}
e &\approx n r_2 \\
&= n (i - r_1)\\
&\approx n (i - \frac in)
\end{align} </math>

[[File:Focus of thin half lens.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|Focusing by a thin planoconvex lens]]
If the incoming ray is parallel to the optical axis and distance <math display="inline">h</math> from it, then 
<math display=block>\sin i = \frac hR \implies i \approx \frac hR.</math>

Substituting into the expression above, one gets
<math display=block>e \approx \frac {h}{R} (n-1).</math>

This ray crosses the optical axis at distance <math>f</math>, given by 
<math display=block>\tan e = \frac hf \implies e \approx \frac hf </math>

Combining the two expressions gives <math display=inline>\frac 1f = \frac 1R (n - 1) </math>.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Durán-Ramírez |first1=Víctor M |last2=Muñoz-Maciel |first2=Jesús |last3=Casillas-Rodríguez |first3=Francisco J |last4=Mora-Gonzalez |first4=Miguel |last5=Peña-Lecona |first5=Francisco G. |title=Exact Equations for the Back and Effective Focal Lengths of a Plano-Concave Thick Lens |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/3149719378 |publisher=University Siegen |access-date=27 December 2025 |date=2024 |id={{ProQuest|3149719378}} }}</ref>

It can be shown that if two such lenses of radii <math display="inline">R_1
</math> and <math display="inline">-R_2
</math> are placed close together, the inverses of the focal lengths can be added up giving the thin lens formula:

<math display=block>\frac 1f = \left(n-1\right)\left( \frac 1{R_1} - \frac 1{R_2} \right)</math>

== Image formation ==
[[File:thin_lens_rays.svg|thumb|Thin lens ray rules]]
Certain [[Ray (optics)|rays]] follow simple rules when passing through a thin lens, in the [[paraxial approximation|paraxial ray approximation]]:
*Any ray that enters parallel to the axis on one side of the lens proceeds towards the [[Focus (optics)|focal point]] <math>f_2</math> on the other side (red in figure). 
*Any ray that arrives at the lens after passing through the focal point <math>f_1</math> on the front side, comes out parallel to the axis on the other side (blue). 
*Any ray that passes through the center of the lens will not change its direction (green).

If three such rays are traced from the same point on an object in front of the lens (such as the top), their intersection will mark the location of the corresponding point on the image of the object. By following the paths of these rays, the relationship between the object distance ''s<sub>o</sub>'' and the image distance ''s<sub>i</sub>'' (these distances are with respect to the lens) can be shown to be
:<math>{1\over s_o} + {1\over s_i} = {1\over f}</math>
which is known as the ''Gaussian thin-lens equation''. The Gaussian thin-lens equation has a sign convention described as follows:<ref>{{Cite book |last=Eugene |first=Hecht |title=Optics |publisher=Pearson |year=2017 |isbn=978-1-292-09693-3 |edition=5th |pages=173 |language=English |chapter=Finite Imagery}}</ref><ref name="pt">{{cite book |last1=Tipler |first1=Paul |title=Physics |date=1976 |publisher=Worth Publishers, Inc. |location=New York |isbn=087901041X |page=650}}</ref>

[[File:thin_lens_graph.svg|thumb|Plots of image distance ''s<sub>i</sub>'' and magnification ''M<sub>T</sub>'' vs object distance ''s<sub>o</sub>'' for the Gaussian lens equation &ndash; the dashed curve denotes a virtual image]]
Plots of image distance ''s<sub>i</sub>'', and magnification ''M<sub>T</sub>'' vs object distance ''s<sub>o</sub>'' are [[hyperbola#Rectangular_hyperbola|rectangular hyperbolas]] with the vertical [[asymptote]] being ''s<sub>o</sub>'' = ''f'', and the horizontal asymptote being ''s<sub>i</sub>'' = ''f'' and ''M<sub>T</sub>'' = 0, respectively. Their positive and negative branches denote the real and virtual images, respectively.<ref>https://pubs.aip.org/aapt/ajp/article-abstract/11/5/293/1033016/The-Graph-of-the-Lens-Equation-in-Three-Variables?redirectedFrom=PDF</ref><ref>https://www.academia.edu/3085661/Missing_hyperbola_and_cardinal_points_of_a_lens_system</ref>

There are other sign conventions such as the [http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/geoopt/lenseq.html#c2 Cartesian sign convention] where the thin lens equation is written as<math display="block">{1\over s_o} + {1\over f} = {1\over s_i}.</math>For a thick lens, the same form of lens equation is applicable with the modification that the image and object distances are measured from the [[Cardinal point (optics)|principal planes]] of the lens.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hecht |first=Eugene |title=Optics |publisher=Pearson |year=2017 |isbn=978-1-292-09693-3 |edition=5th |location= |pages=257 |language=English |chapter=Chapter 6.1 Thick Lenses and Lens Systems}}</ref>

==Physical optics==
In scalar wave optics, a lens is a part which shifts the phase of the wavefront. Mathematically this can be understood as a multiplication of the wavefront with the following function:<ref>
{{cite book
 |last=Saleh |first=B.E.A.
 |year=2007
 |title=Fundamentals of Photonics
 |edition=2nd
 |publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons|Wiley]]
}}</ref>

<!-- Note that there are arbitrary sign conventions involved in many optics expressions. The correct sign depends on the definitions chosen. Don't assume a sign is wrong just because it disagrees with the book you're using.-->
:<math>\exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{\lambda} \frac{r^2}{2f}\right)</math>.
